articles.title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
articles.summary: Should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences?
articles.body:
Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.

For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.

Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.

Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."

That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.

Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".

Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.

"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.

Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.

As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?

For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.

Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.

In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally.

Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.

In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.

Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.

The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.

Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.

Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.

The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each.

There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.

Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.

Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.

Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.

"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."

Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.

"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."

"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."

One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.

This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.

Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.

Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.

Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."

Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.

Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.

David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?

He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.

This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.

Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low-energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".

Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered £2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the £7,500 for a heating-only model.

Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands.

In Scotland homeowners can also get a £7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households.

Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and new builds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed.

Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave.

She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in.

Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures … due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool".

Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it.

Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat.

The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year.

There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness.

Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney.

The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street.

And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment.

The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect – the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning.

And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down.

But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment.

The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road.

Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise.

Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand.

In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun."

"It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results."

The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by.

"It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me."

Meanwhile, Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum.

"We sit there all day with it on, it helps so much I want one in my flat."

articles.title: Urban League report says Trump administration is harming Black Americans’ chances at American Dream
articles.summary: The report says the challenges it highlights for Black communities are warning signs for the prosperity of all Americans.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The American Dream may not be dead for many Black Americans, but it is further away than at any point since the Civil Rights Movement, warns a report by the National Urban League. Released on Thursday, the annual “State of Black America” report grimly describes Black Americans’ economic and political prospects as having worsened due to policy changes from President Donald Trump’s administration, according to a copy obtained by The Associated Press. The report contends that the challenges it highlights for Black communities are warning signs for the prosperity of all Americans. “It may be the focus is us, but the impact is not just us,” said Marc Morial, president and CEO of the National Urban League. “While they have targeted and focused on Black Americans, these attacks are going to impact broadly working Americans, poor Americans, aspirational middle-class Americans, and this is what this report points to.” Tracing the arc of American history, the Urban League describes Black Americans’ struggle for emancipation from slavery and equal economic and political rights as a gruesome but optimistic part of the American story. Now, the report says, the Trump administration is at odds with the goals and achievements of the Civil Rights Movement, citing the overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, as well as the president’s focus on overhauling voting laws through the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, as examples of rollbacks of long-sought civil rights policies. The report’s authors offer policy and strategy recommendations for civil rights groups aiming to combat the Trump administration. “The civil rights community must consolidate its legal resistance and turn courtroom wins into durable policy,” the report says. “The movement must build economic infrastructure that doesn’t depend on the goodwill of any one administration.” Report contributors include potential Democratic presidential contender This year’s report includes contributions from members of Congress, and policy and legal experts, as well as some media personalities. U.S. Sens. Angela Alsobrooks, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Raphael Warnock all contributed to the report, as well as Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott. Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey contributed a video message to the report. Moore, who is widely viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender, submitted an essay focused on closing the racial wealth gap and Black Americans’ history of economic advancement in the face of adversity. “With wisdom and grit, my mom was able to lift me and my family to a higher rung on the economic ladder. But too often wisdom and grit aren’t enough,” Moore wrote. He later called closing the racial wealth gap “a matter of moral clarity” but cautioned that “government alone cannot close the racial wealth gap. It’s going to take all of us,” referencing the private sector and civil society. Report blasts ‘economic assault’ on Black Americans Whether corporate America and major nonprofits are still willing to participate is an open question. The report condemns the Trump administration’s efforts to roll back diversity initiatives and economic advancement projects in the private sector, and expressed frustration with companies that cooperated with an “economic assault” on Americans, especially Black Americans. “This has been a campaign of coercion and oppression directed at these institutions who have been out here working hard to, if you will, change America,” Morial said. “The important thing about companies is that every company has not bent the knee. Some may have done some cosmetic changes. Some have been in full and complete retreat.” The DEI rollbacks are a jarring reversal for the Urban League, which held sway in the Biden White House on economic and social policies. The report lauds President Joe Biden’s administration for signing a sweeping Covid-19 stimulus package, as well as laws supporting minority small businesses and a bipartisan infrastructure bill. “Not every promise was kept, and the current administration is pushing to roll our wins back, but these wins serve as a blueprint for what is possible through sustained advocacy and a clear vision,” the authors write. The agenda, the Urban League declares, was “the most consequential federal investments in Black America since the Great Society.” The organization and its civil rights allies now find themselves in a strikingly different political environment under the Trump administration. “Looking at our current political landscape, the calls for racial healing and righting of this nation’s wrongs in the aftermath of the murder of George Floyd feel like a fever dream,” the report reads. But the study also acknowledges that Black Americans have overcome more dire and discriminatory moments. Report is Urban League’s 50th edition The Urban League’s inaugural 1976 report on the state of Black America was described by The New York Times at the time as “a profoundly depressing document” that laid out the persistent disparities between the economic outlooks of Black and white Americans, a decade after the Civil Rights Movement’s crowning achievements were signed into law. The report was established as a response to that year’s State of the Union address by President Gerald R. Ford and the Democratic response, neither of which mentioned the economic outlooks for Black Americans. The report offered policy recommendations on crime, education, housing, social services and general economic policy. “It is a document that does not attempt to cover up the seriousness of the situation black people find themselves in,” the authors wrote at the time. Several of its recommendations were later taken up by President Jimmy Carter, who was elected to the White House months after the report’s release. This year’s 50th anniversary document echoes the frustration found in the inaugural report. While Morial acknowledged that the Urban League’s assessments may lead to pessimism, he urged Americans concerned about civil rights and economic progress to respond at the ballot box and with their pocketbooks. “We cannot be dejected. We cannot be cynical. We must act,” Morial said. “We have to fight to make sure that those that are really trying to kill the essence of the American dream don’t win.”

articles.title: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson defends ousting Police Chief Shon Barnes after shootout
articles.summary: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson on Friday defended her decision to oust the city’s police chief as the “right decision at the right time,” but she declined to explain why.
articles.body: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson on Friday defended her decision to oust the city’s police chief as the “right decision at the right time,” but she declined to explain why. The leadership change came as police continue searching for people involved in a fatal, gang-related shootout at a food festival near the Space Needle last weekend. A 15-year-old was arrested at the scene and has been charged with assault, but charging documents say the gun he was seen firing wasn’t involved in the deaths of two bystanders. Wilson and then-Police Chief Shon Barnes faced criticism for being slow to release key information about the shootout on Sunday, including whether suspects remained at large. Barnes, who was the city’s second Black police chief, has been credited with boosting the recruitment of officers and helping reduce crime downtown. A number of Black community organizations, a major business group and several City Council members issued statements criticizing Wilson’s decision to replace him Thursday. At a news conference Friday with Andre Sayles, a Seattle deputy chief the mayor named as interim chief, Wilson credited Barnes for his service and said that as mayor she had a clearer window into the operations at the Seattle Police Department than her critics. The lack of communication about a mass shooting at a major public event in Seattle was not the only reason she asked Barnes to resign, she said. “There were multiple factors,” Wilson said. “The events of Sunday played into it.” Sayles told the news conference the department would boost police staffing at public festivals for the remainder of the summer. He also said he believed investigators are close to finding and arresting additional suspects in the shootout. The gunfire erupted in the waning hours of the Bite of Seattle, an annual three-day festival that draws hundreds of food and retail vendors and performers. Three people, including a suspect, were killed, and four people were wounded. One of the people injured was a 2-year-old boy.

articles.title: Sir John Curtice: The "Burnham bounce" is real but it's not massive
articles.summary: The governing party's poll ratings have improved but they're only just ahead of Reform.
articles.body:
The consistent message of the opinion polls since the new prime minister walked into Downing Street almost a fortnight ago is that Labour is enjoying a "Burnham bounce". And this has now been confirmed by the party's convincing victory in Thursday's Greater Manchester mayoral by-election.

Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down.

But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence.

The Burnham boost is far from unprecedented.

All but one of the recent mid-term changes of prime minister have been followed by an increase in the popularity of the incumbent government. Support for Labour rose by seven points after Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair in 2007, while the Conservatives enjoyed a six-point bounce when Boris Johnson took over from Theresa May in 2019. Only Liz Truss' arrival in Downing Street in 2022 â which was overshadowed by the death shortly thereafter of Queen Elizabeth II â failed to give her party a boost.

We should also bear in mind the depth of the electoral hole that Burnham has inherited as Labour leader. The 19% at which Labour stood when Sir Keir resigned was the lowest poll rating passed on by any prime minister departing mid-term â even lower than the 23% bequeathed by Liz Truss when she resigned after just 45 days in office.

Against that backdrop, it would have been very surprising indeed if the replacement of the deeply unpopular Sir Keir by the relatively popular Burnham had not given Labour a short-term boost. However, even after Burnham's bounce, his party's poll average is still the lowest for any newly minted mid-term PM, while the party is still well adrift in the polls of the (relatively low) 35% it won at the 2024 general election.

That said, Labour's victory in Thursday's Manchester mayoral by-election was convincing. True, Labour's 47% share of the first preference vote was well down on the 63% that Burnham secured in the last mayoral contest shortly before the 2024 general election. However, not only did it represent a near doubling of the 24% that Labour registered across the region in May's local elections, but also it was even four points up on Labour's tally locally in the 2024 general election â and thus a much better performance than would have been anticipated from even the latest national polling.

But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.

Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.

This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.

In the Manchester by-election, Reform's share of the first preference vote was nine point down on its tally across the region in May's local elections. As in the Makerfield by-election, the party seemingly suffered from the advance made by Rupert Lowe's breakaway from Reform, Restore Britain, which won nearly 9% of the Manchester vote, outpolling the Conservatives in the process.

But for Reform's difficulties, the "Burnham bounce" would probably have been insufficient to put Labour in the lead in the national polls.

The principal source of that bounce has been clawing voters back from the Greens and the Liberal Democrats, both of whom have suffered a two-point drop since Burnham's uncontested victory in the Labour leadership contest. For the Greens â much of whose increased support in recent months came from disappointed 2024 Labour voters â the change of prime minister has proven particularly damaging. The Greens' current 11% tally is as much as four points adrift of where it was when Sir Keir announced he was leaving.

When he resigned, 14% of Labour's 2024 election voters said they would now back the Greens. That figure is now 9%.

Winning back former Labour voters has generally been a key component of the Burnham bounce. Overall, 67% of those who voted Labour in 2024 now say they would vote for the party, compared to 57% when Sir Keir indicated he was leaving Downing Street.

Following Farage's difficulties, Labour is also now losing fewer of its 2024 voters to Reform. But the same is true of the Conservatives, whose loss of support to Reform in the polls during this Parliament has always been much greater than that suffered by Labour. Far from suffering from a Burnham bounce, Kemi Badenoch's party has edged up to 20% in the polls for the first time since last spring.

Burnham's arrival has given Labour new hope. But despite having overtaken Reform in the polls, the new Labour leader still has to prove he can win back the working class pro-Brexit voters that Labour once regarded as its core vote but who now form the heart of support for Reform.

To do this â and put Labour on course for victory in 2029 - Burnham needs to deliver on the policy challenges facing his government, which remain as formidable as those that beset Sir Keir. Labour's prospects at the next election will ultimately depend on whether voters have come to believe that what he has said he will do is actually happening.

John Curtice is a professor of politics at Strathclyde University and senior fellow at the National Centre for Social Research and The UK in a Changing Europe

articles.title: How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight fire
articles.summary: As Europe faces its worst wildfires in decades, Australia offers lessons in disaster preparedness.
articles.body:
The wildfires currently ravaging Europe feel close to home for Professor Marta Yebra, despite being on the other side of the world.

Originally from Spain, the Canberra-based bushfire expert has spent years developing ways for Australia - home to some of the most fire-prone landscapes in the world - to battle its own blazes.

She heads up the Bushfire Research Centre of Excellence, which was set up in the aftermath of Australia's worst fire season on record: the Black Summer fires of 2019-20 , which razed a combined area about the size of the UK.

Her team looks at how technology such as satellites, drones and AI can be used to better detect fires, alongside the knowledge of experienced firefighters.

Equally important, though, is the knowledge and experience that has accrued in Australia over thousands of years, and has been passed down through generations.

This is where Australia has an advantage.

The use of fire has been part of the country's Indigenous culture since long before Europeans arrived in the 18th century - but the value of this ingrained knowledge has only been truly realised in recent years.

Yebra has spearheaded an innovative project, bringing together millennia-old knowledge in Australia's Indigenous communities with cutting-edge satellite imagery to help detect where fires are most likely to break out.

The satellite images pick up the "fuel moisture content" in the landscape, which signals where there might be a large amount of fuel, such as dry leaves, grass, shrubs and bark. But such data provides just one part of a bigger picture.

That's where the likes of Adrian Webster come in.

Growing up on the south coast of New South Wales (NSW), Webster learnt how to read the environment or "country" - the term Indigenous Australians use for their ancestral homeland – from his elders.

Using Indigenous ecological knowledge – a plant's colour and scent, for example, or the shade cover of trees - he can verify information in the satellite images from Yebra's team.

"She had all this amazing data, but there was no translation to what it meant on the ground, so it was kind of useless," he explains.

"But through an Indigenous perspective, it was not useless. It was a map that could guide you through the country and, if you understood it, take you directly into a place that is ready to burn."

For Webster, assessing the land involves him "literally digging and going underground," he says.

"We're looking at the subsurface level and then everything from that up beyond the canopy."

Yebra said there was a "remarkable agreement" between Webster's local knowledge and the satellite data, demonstrating the combined value of Indigenous expertise and Western science.

Her team now hopes to get more funding for the project, and work with Indigenous communities to co-design plans to protect the land and manage fires.

For Webster, it's about "allowing our mother – the planet Earth – a voice again".

Another example of ancient wisdom influencing modern techniques can be found in the way Australia fights fire with fire.

Cultural burning refers to a longstanding practice by Indigenous Australians to manage the environment while also maintaining a deep, spiritual connection to the land.

Part of it is lighting "cool fires": small, controlled blazes that create a patchy landscape, so fuel does not build up in one area.

"In Europe, there is no such cultural aspect to this kind of landscape planning," Yebra says.

Wildfire scientists in Spain have blamed a massive build-up of fuel for the blazes currently devastating the country.

"It is difficult to watch what is happening in Spain, but it is not surprising," Yebra says. "Particularly as climate change is increasing the frequency of extreme fire weather across southern Europe."

She believes Europe, facing its worst wildfires in decades , could benefit from Australia's firefighting experience.

"We have decades of experience living with large and high-intensity bushfires," she says. "One of the biggest changes we are seeing in bushfire management is a shift from simply reacting to fires towards anticipating risk and acting earlier.

"The earlier we can identify risk or detect an ignition, the more options firefighters have."

Webster says a key lesson the world could learn from Australia is "don't sit back and wait".

"The longer you leave it, the more fuel there is to burn, so the fire is naturally going to be bigger and harder to extinguish," he says.

"Indigenous people always knew that, so we burnt continuously all the time. That way there was no fuel for big fires."

The practice of lighting cool fires dates back 60,000 years. Part of Webster's role is to assess the area before one is lit, looking for natural signs of oil and water in the landscape so that the blaze remains under control.

"All the answers are in the environment," he says. "There's a sweet spot in the middle where there's enough water to slow that fire down but there's enough oil to push that fire on."

A more modern tactic used across Australia is a prescribed burn, also known as a hazard reduction burn. These carefully planned, often large-scale fires are usually carried out during cooler months, and are increasingly being adopted in parts of Europe.

It's an approach that has become especially vital in the "urban fringes", says superintendent Andrew Shurety from Fire and Rescue NSW.

As Australia's population grows and suburbs expand, more people are moving closer to bushland, making hazard burns firefighters' "main mitigating factor that we try to do to reduce the risk of bushfires because we know they're going to come".

The problem, Shurety points out, is that longer fire seasons and more rain during cooler months shortens the window that such burns can be carried out.

Starving a fire of fuel is also the idea behind "backburning", a widely accepted practice in Australia where a blaze is deliberately lit ahead of a main fire to strip out the vegetation and try to stop it from spreading.

This approach is also being increasingly adopted overseas - as Queensland firefighter Damian Hatfield found out.

When he travelled to Alberta, Canada with a contingent of Australian firefighters to help tackle the country's worst wildfires on record, backburning was not widely used. A year later, things had shifted.

"Backburning was definitely much more at the forefront when I returned in 2024," he says, with Canadian firefighters showing "no hesitation" to include the approach in their operations.

Drones have also transformed how Australia deals with bushfires, says Trent Curtin, from the Rural Fire Service in NSW - particularly in recent years.

"The local crews arrive, send a drone up quickly, have a look at where the fire is and how it's progressing, get some intelligence and make decisions before we can even get our large helicopters or other aircraft down," Curtin explains.

Drones also deliver heavy gear to crews on the ground, start blazes for backburning operations and help assess the damage caused by fires.

Back at Yebra's centre, the team's work is particularly timely with weather forecasters predicting a super El Nino this summer - which could increase the probability of extreme heat, drought and bushfires.

"Our next fire season is looking like it's going to be a bad one," Yebra says.

That concern is shared by Jason Heffernan, chief officer of the Country Fire Authority in Australia's southeastern state of Victoria. Here, the memories of 2009's Black Saturday bushfires – the country's deadliest on record – loom large.

"For this summer coming, we're bracing for what could be something extremely significant," Heffernan says.

Even in the broader scheme of things, he notes that local fire seasons are starting earlier and lasting longer. "Unfortunately for Australia", he adds, "our environment is designed to burn."

But as the world braces for wildfires that are more frequent and intense, Heffernan also believes "we must take a global perspective".

"No fire service can do this on their own and the key is to have formal and trusted networks," he says - as well as national and international resource-sharing arrangements.

One of the challenges as a fire chief, he explains, is knowing when to ask for help - too late and the benefits will be lost, but too early and resources might be wasted.

Such a call was made just earlier this week, when France sent its first-ever request for help from Australian firefighters. Two dozen crew and several aircraft will be deployed as France battles record-breaking wildfires amid a prolonged summer heatwave.

Australia regularly sends specialist teams to the US and Canada, and vice versa, with many requests for what's known as "arduous fire crews": those who have fought fires in rugged and remote areas.

There are far fewer requests from Europe, Heffernan says - but this may change as "the global fire community is becoming more connected".

As he points out, while forests and climates vary across the globe, "we're seeing bushfires occur in parts of the world that never had bushfires before".

articles.title: Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections and protests – all you need to know
articles.summary: Protests over refugee seats turn deadly, forcing staggered elections under internet blackout and calls for a boycott.
articles.body:
Pakistan-administered Kashmir is facing its worst political crisis in years after weeks of protests demanding electoral reforms turned deadly.

The protests forced staggered regional elections, with the second of the three-phase vote held on Sunday amid calls for a boycott by local activists and a shutdown of businesses in Muzaffarabad, the region’s main city, and other places.

list 1 of 4 Pakistan-administered Kashmir opens polls in violence-wracked election

list 2 of 4 Protest group says 30 dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir vote unrest

list 3 of 4 Pakistan’s Kashmir votes: Why the election hinges on 12 disputed seats

list 4 of 4 Is Pakistan ‘using India’s playbook’ in Kashmir?

The third and final round of voting is scheduled for August 10.

The protests are led by the Jammu and Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a banned group pushing for changes to electoral laws and more economic concessions for the region.

The epicentre of the protests is Rawalakot, the headquarters of the Poonch division in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), one of the two regions that comprise Pakistan-administered Kashmir, the other being Gilgit-Baltistan.

The AJK region has its own legislature, but it is not a full-fledged province within Pakistan because of the dispute over the Kashmir territory with neighbouring India.

Muzaffarabad, AJK’s capital, is about 30km (18.5 miles) from the Line of Control, the de facto border dividing Kashmir between Pakistan and India.

Residents and local estimates say the death toll has surpassed 50, including seven law enforcement personnel. No official figures have been released. Protest leaders claim more than 60 civilians have died in less than two months.

There has been a partial internet blackout since June 5, according to NetBlocks, an independent observer.

According to iVerify , the fact-checking wing at the Center of Excellence in Journalism (CEJ) in Karachi, telecommunications are limited and internet connectivity is sparse in AJK.

Protesters are demanding more political rights and an end to policies they believe undermine local representation in the legislature. The government says the movement is threatening public order in the region.

Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director-general of Pakistan’s Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of Pakistan’s army, on Friday told a news conference that “Kashmiris hold a special place in Pakistan’s heart” and accused vested interests in India of attempting to create unrest. New Delhi has rejected the allegation.

Chaudhry said the state has the sole authority to use force and that violence by any group was unacceptable. He said the government was exercising “wisdom and restraint” in maintaining peace and stability.

During his press conference, Chaudhry did not mention the number of civilian casualties in the region.

Though the protests started in June, their foundation was laid the month before. Here is a timeline:

Late May 2026: Talks between JAAC and the government in Muzaffarabad collapse over demands to abolish 12 seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly.

The seats in the legislature are reserved for Kashmiri refugees who migrated to Pakistan after 1947 and now live outside the region.

The JAAC says the arrangement allows Pakistan-based political parties to influence the government of Pakistan-administered Kashmir while diverting development funds intended for the region.

June 5: Authorities designate JAAC a “proscribed organisation” under the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Anti-Terrorism Act, 2014.

Internet and mobile services are suspended across the region, and officials advise nonresidents not to travel to AJK between June 5 and June 20, urging tourists already there to leave.

June 7: The AJK Supreme Court rules that the 12 refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

June 8: Clashes erupt between protesters and security forces in Rawalakot and nearby areas. Regional authorities and local media report that 11 people are killed and several injured, including protesters and security personnel.

Federal paramilitary forces are deployed across the region.

June 9: JAAC calls a regionwide general strike. Markets, schools and public transport shut down across much of AJK.

Mid-June: Weeks of strikes, sit-ins and clashes continue in Poonch division, as the death toll crosses 20. JAAC protests in Rawalakot and nearby areas, while the rest of the AJK remains tense but calm.

July 21: The AJK Election Commission announces a revised three-phase election schedule in response to the unrest. Voting is announced for July 27 in Mirpur division, August 2 in Muzaffarabad division and for the 12 disputed refugee seats, and on August 10 in Poonch division.

July 27: The first phase of voting is held in Mirpur division, with early results favouring Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N). On the same day, thousands join a JAAC-led march from Rawalakot towards Muzaffarabad. Deadly clashes erupt again with security forces.

August 2: The second round of voting is held in Muzaffarabad division amid calls for a boycott and limited access to internet.

Are the protests aimed at JAK’s independence?

No, the protests are being held against the reservation of 12 seats in Pakistan-administered Kashmir’s legislature for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir who now live in other parts of Pakistan.

The JAAC accuses Islamabad of using these seats to manipulate local politics – accusations rejected by the national government.

The JAAC says all seats in the legislature must go to those who actually reside in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, and not to people living in other constituencies scattered across Pakistan.

Experts say the crisis is part of a deeper, long-running debate about governance, political representation, resource allocation and regional autonomy in Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

The Jammu and Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKJAAC), commonly known as JAAC, is a grassroots coalition of civil society groups, traders, lawyers and activists formed in 2023 in the AJK area of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

Rather than being led by a single figure, the JAAC operates as a coalition with several spokespeople, including Shaukat Nawaz Mir, Sardar Umar Nazir, Khawaja Mehran Arshad and Sardar Aman Khan. Mir was arrested in late June after the regional government banned the JAAC.

Following the ban, authorities placed all four spokespeople on a wanted list, offering a reward of 10 million Pakistani rupees ($36,000) for information leading to their arrests.

The JAAC first staged a protest in May 2023 against soaring electricity bills, alleged smuggling of flour and shortages of subsidised wheat.

The movement reached its first major flashpoint in May 2024 , when protesters marched towards Muzaffarabad. Violent clashes with security forces killed at least five people, including a police officer.

The demonstrations ended after the government agreed to a series of economic concessions, marking a big victory for the JAAC.

In September and October 2025, the JAAC unveiled a 38-point charter of demands and launched a regionwide shutdown, prompting authorities to impose a communications blackout.

The charter remains at the centre of the current unrest. Its demands include economic subsidies, investigations into alleged corruption, improved social services and infrastructure, and the abolition of the 12 reserved assembly seats.

AJK’s incumbent Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore is from the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), which is part of the federal coalition government led by PML-N’s Sharif.

PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, the son of slain former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, says 35 of the 38 demands of the JAAC have been implemented, arguing that the remaining proposals are either unfeasible or blocked by court rulings.

Rights group Amnesty International said on July 28 that at least 40 people have been killed, including 34 protesters and six police and paramilitary personnel. The group has demanded a “transparent investigation” into the use of force against protesters.

Residents and local estimates say the death toll has surpassed 50, although officials have not confirmed the figure.

Amid a partial internet blackout, disinformation has further clouded the situation. Viral videos and images claiming to show staged protester injuries, fake police shootings, and AI-generated evidence have circulated widely.

Fact-checkers at iVerify Pakistan have confirmed some visuals as authentic while debunking others as AI-generated or recycled footage. However, many claims remain difficult to verify due to restricted access and the ongoing communications blackout.

Road blockades have also cut off towns, disrupting travel, work and access to healthcare.

Markets, schools and public transport have repeatedly remained shut during the regionwide strikes, while tourism has suffered after authorities urged visitors to leave.

articles.title: The real reason child vaccination rates are falling
articles.summary: As child immunisation rates fall across the UK, one clinic in west Yorkshire is taking aggressive steps to boost immunisations
articles.body:
Twenty-week-old Grayson easily could have become one of the tens of thousands of British babies left unvaccinated against polio.

His mother, Lily, agrees with the principle of immunisation. But overwhelmed by the early weeks of motherhood, and suffering from post-partum depression after a traumatic birth, she was daunted by the prospect of a long journey to a doctor's surgery. "I've been through the trenches, awake all night. You don't want to leave the house, or go to a different town."

Weeks ticked by, and eventually Grayson missed the polio and diphtheria jabs he was supposed to get at eight weeks old. By that point he was officially classed by the NHS as "overdue" for vaccination; effectively, he was on his GP's naughty list.

Then Lily realised there was a clinic practically on her doorstep - at a location she hadn't expected.

That clinic - in Keighley, West Yorkshire - runs from a vacant retail unit at the Airedale shopping centre, a 1960s-era precinct that locals say has fallen on hard times in recent years, with plenty of empty, boarded-up units. The staff who created the clinic thought: why not use one of those vacant units to administer vaccines?

"This was an empty shop; there was nothing here, the windows were all blacked out," Flora Jennings, a local charity coordinator, tells me over the sound of a baby's laughter, on the morning I visit the clinic.

It's an imaginative solution to a national problem. Over the last 15 years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across Britain. The share of five-year-olds in England who have received a four-in-one jab (which protects against viruses like polio and tetanus) is now 81%, down from 89% in 2014. About 84% have received both of their recommended MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) jabs, down from 88% a decade ago.

"If you just look at the generalised population, the decline doesn't look horrific," says Prof Dan Hungerford, an epidemiologist at the University of Liverpool who gave evidence to Parliament on this topic. "But if you compare us to other nations, particularly our European neighbours, we are one of the worst-performing countries in terms of getting early-life vaccinations to children."

Politicians are now asking how Britain - the country of Edward Jenner, the "father of immunology" - could have allowed its immunisation rates to drop so low, and what could fix it.

One Labour MP on the Health Committee has gone further, telling the BBC that it's time to consider a policy that's commonplace in some countries, but still something of a taboo in Britain: mandatory childhood immunisations.

Before the 1800s, between 40% and 50% of children in Europe died before their 15th birthday. Now, in Britain that number is well below 1%, according to the UN.

Scientists broadly agree that vaccines were key to this improvement.

"Along with clean water and sanitation, immunisations have had a profound impact on keeping children alive," says Ben Kasstan-Dabush, a lecturer in global health policy at the University of Edinburgh.

And that's why some find it so worrying that Britain's rates have slipped. Last year alone saw measles outbreaks in parts of Birmingham, Bristol, and north London; so far this year, two children in England have died of the disease.

In January, MPs on the Health Committee described the backslide as "national disgrace".

Some blame the rise of misinformation on social media. Last year, a group of American scientists found that reading just one anti-vax Facebook comment about the HPV jab - given to teenagers - was enough to make some parents hesitate.

But all of the public health experts who spoke to the BBC said that whilst anti-vax social media sentiment plays its part, they don't think it's the main reason immunisation rates have slipped.

Instead, they point to something more mundane: they think that parents of young children simply have fewer face-to-face contacts with medical professionals than they did 10 or 15 years ago.

Beccy Baird, a senior fellow at the King's Fund think tank, says that despite colourful media reporting around "anti-vaxxers", most parents who turn down vaccination are not ideologically opposed to it. Convenience plays a big role, she says; vaccination rates are highest when parents regularly interact with medics, who can remind them to get their children jabbed and tell them exactly where to do it.

And those interactions have become rarer. England has seen a 45% decline over the last decade in the number of health visitors (nurses and midwives who treat young children at their home), according to BBC analysis. It's part of a health visitor's job to remind parents about vaccines and, in some cases, administer jabs directly.

And over roughly the same period, the number of fully trained GPs in England struggled to keep up with rising patient demand, according to British Medical Association data; while the Nuffield Trust think tank suggests that patients have become less likely to see the same GP on repeated visits - meaning families don't build trusted relationships with doctors they recognise.

"Those touch points have become fewer," says Kasstan-Dabush.

At Keighley's shopping centre, inside the vaccination clinic, nurses are passing around biscuits.

"The kitchen's there, the playpen's there," says Jennings as she points to a soft-play where parents can leave children while their siblings are vaccinated. "I wanted it to be really inviting, almost like you're walking into someone's home."

The idea of opening a vaccination clinic inside a town centre shopping arcade seemed odd to some of the staff when it was first suggested.

Now, they say it's key to the clinic's success. "We need to make it simple, we need to put services where people come," says Jennings. It means they can catch casual shoppers who "pop their head around the door" and decide on a whim to get their child vaccinated.

"We're right in the centre. And down here it's flat, so you don't have to push a pram up a hill." She says some parents simply won't attend a clinic if it involves more than one bus.

And in the families come. Over the morning, the clinic vaccinates 10 infants, some of whom are classed by the NHS as "overdue". In many cases, the parents actually turn up to use a different service, like baby weighing, but once they are inside, lead GP Dr Zoyah Hussain gently suggests an immunisation - and most parents say yes.

"I do get a lot of questionsâ¦ 'why do we need to give them jabs?', 'why don't we just let nature manage itself?'," Hussain says.

There's Lily, the 18-year-old who finally gets her son Grayson his polio and diphtheria jabs. And there's Keeley, an assistant in a ceramics shop, who arrives with her baby Luca, and is impressed by the clinic's convenience, with no need for an 08:00 phone call or complicated online form. "It's easy-peasy," she says.

Most of the young mothers have come across online anti-vax posts. "I see these things on Facebook where it's like, don't give your child vaccines because it's got ADHD in them," says Lily. Indeed, Hussain says she still hears parents asking if the MMR jab causes autism, a full 28 years after a link was suggested in a now-discredited paper by the former doctor Andrew Wakefield.

The clinic - which serves a relatively poor community - has vaccinated hundreds of infants since 2023, helping to boost coverage in an area that's historically had a low rate of immunisations. As of March this year, 88% of the children registered with Modality AWC (the GP practice that runs the clinic) now receive their first MMR dose by the age of 18 months, up from 78% three years ago.

"We are bucking that national trend," says Bill Graham, a senior administrator at the practice.

So what can be done about falling vaccination rates across the rest of the country?

One option is to emulate the Keighley model, and open walk-in clinics in vacant retail units. Jennings argues there are crumbling shopping centres all over the country, hit by online shopping, that could do the job.

Baird, from the King's Fund, agrees that vaccination works best when it's carried out in small, easy-to-access local venues - like shopping centres - rather than large, intimidating vaccine hubs that might involve a long journey. In a paper, she studied the roll-out of Covid vaccines in Gloucestershire - and found that "vaccines delivered locally throughâ¦ familiar community venues - instead of mass-vaccination centres - made access easier, more trusted".

She says: "If you put it in Tesco car park, people will get it."

But some experts are sceptical. Whilst schemes like Keighley's can help on the margins, they say, at the national level a much bigger answer is needed. Hungerford says that child poverty is a key driver of vaccine refusal; parents who have to worry about bills often don't have the brain space to think about immunisations, he says.

And some are pushing for more radical solutions.

Labour MP Paulette Hamilton, a former nurse who was recently interim chair of Parliament's Health Committee, tells the BBC it's time for a "national conversation" on whether child vaccinations should be "opt out" rather than "opt in" (though she stresses she is not speaking on behalf of the committee).

"We were a country that was free of some of these childhood illnesses, and now it's just getting really bad," she says. "The conversation should be about, do you get a small payment [for getting your child vaccinated]? Do you make it mandatory, so you opt out rather than opt in? Is it that we need more education?."

She didn't specify what an "opt out" policy would look like, but various US states already do it. In Texas, a child needs certain vaccinations to attend school, unless their parent fills out a government-issued form explaining a moral, religious, or medical exemption. Supporters say these policies capture the "casual refuseniks" - people who aren't particularly opposed to vaccination, but simply don't make the effort to get their child jabbed.

Other places go further. In Germany, parents can be fined if their children aren't jabbed against measles. Under Australia's "no jab, no pay" policy, parents who refuse immunisations are denied certain benefits.

But those tough, coercive policies leave some uncomfortable. "Mandatory vaccination has been steered away from in the UK for good reason," says Hungerford. For one thing, he thinks, "you risk excluding vulnerable people from things like childcare."

Others say that barring unvaccinated children from school is only likely to alienate their parents further from healthcare, amplifying their mistrust of authority.

At the Keighley shopping centre, Bill Graham says he doesn't think a mandatory approach would work in his corner of Yorkshire. "I think it destroys trust. Healthcare in Britain is based on trust. Maybe the trust isn't quite where it was again 10, 15 years ago, but we're not going to build that up by mandating healthcare."

All that said, experts stress that there's still a degree of mystery about Britain's vaccination problem.

Some parents who refuse jabs simply won't say why - and they're the same groups (poor, lower levels of educational attainment) who are hard to reach via surveys.

This becomes apparent towards the end of my morning at the clinic, when a couple in their thirties arrive to have their baby weighed. Hussain quickly notices that their 23-week-old hasn't had any of his recommended jabs - and asks if they might consider it. The couple glance at each other and quietly shake their heads.

They don't give a reason, and they turn down my request for an interview (the only parents who do so).

Still, Hussain hopes their conversation might have planted a seed. "I've sent her some information. Giving them a platform to speak about their concerns can help.

"It's not us forcing it on anyone. This is a choice."

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: President Trump’s triple bogey
articles.summary: Trump ordered a major escalation of combat with Iran last weekend only to call it off via Truth Social, marking his second reversal on IRGC operations.
articles.body: Pardon the extended analogy ahead, but as President Donald Trump is easily the best golfer among all presidents, it plays well. Don’t believe me about the best golfer assessment? Ask ChatGPT or any AI agent. It isn’t even remotely a close question. Having been a caddy since 1966, I’ve carried lots of clubs, raked plenty of traps and held many pins. "Pipeline Joe Day" was the best senior I’ve ever caddied for, and he earned his nickname among the golf gophers because he drove 16 or 17 out of 18 fairways or greens well into his 80s, but as he lost distance when he crossed over the octogenarian mark, the birdies mostly went away. Even the best short games among seniors can save par but won’t make many birdies. TRUMP IS WINNING EVERY BATTLE IN IRAN—AND RISKING THE WAR THAT MATTERS President Trump can routinely shave a stroke off of par on any given hole, and it wouldn’t surprise if there is an eagle or two every month of rounds. But, as no golfer is perfect, the president is bound to have had some awful rounds and some very bad holes. Not "Tin Cup" Kevin Costner bad, but bad. He must go "OB" on his drive at least occasionally, and a three putt on top of hitting three off the tee… well, that’s usually triple bogey land for even very good amateurs and most pros. Like even the greatest golfers, every president yanks a decision or three almost every round. If a president has ever had a perfect month of perfect days, I’m unaware of it. So mistakes will be made, and President Trump made a big one this past weekend. TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE "Reliable reports from a variety of sources confirm that President Trump had ordered a major escalation of combat with Iran for this past weekend only to call it off late Saturday night. Some of our allies were primed to participate, but others urged a delay." It is the second time President Trump has called off a return to major combat operations that would continue uninterrupted for the weeks it would take to try and break the rump regime in Iran run by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Pay almost no attention to the civilian puppets of the rump regime. It is a military dictatorship inside Iran now. "We just want to win," President Trump declared at the Cabinet meeting in Camp David last week. That was a clear and candid declaration of the end game: A return to the genuinely open Strait of Hormuz coupled with a verifiable abandonment of the Iranian regime’s decades-long drive for nuclear weapons. MORNING GLORY: PRESIDENT TRUMP, IRAN AND NAPOLEON’S STILL-RELEVANT MAXIM President Trump knows that the IRGC lies and that the IRGC cheats. He has said many times that the regime’s negotiators will spend hours talking about the nuclear program in closed meetings, and then immediately walk to the microphones and declare the nuclear program was not discussed at all in the same meetings. "They are scum," he has said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has declared, "These people are crazy." Both are correct. The original MOU was worth a try. I always thought it signaled halftime in the battle and that after the midterm elections in the U.S., President Trump would demand the immediate implementation of a rigorous inspections regime at every site known or suspected of harboring part of Iran’s nuclear weapons program — including "Pickaxe Mountain" — as the necessary conditions without which major combat operations would resume and continue indefinitely to batter the shaky regime until it crumbled in real time. But the IRGC came out of the locker room first and broke the MOU. Since then, they have again broken an agreement to trade a ceasefire for an open Strait and layered on a surprise attack on our military in Jordan. They are the polar opposite of "good faith" bargainers and always have been. There is no reason to believe that the IRGC will not lie and cheat again. It is who they are and who they have always been since Ayatollah Khomeini led the revolution to topple the Shah in 1979. articles.title: HMP Erlestoke prisoners using art as part of rehabilitation
articles.summary: Inmates say it is "rewarding" to create artwork and sell it online with the help of a charity.
articles.body:
A charity is supporting the rehabilitation of prisoners by offering them the opportunity to create and sell their own artwork.

Prisoners at HMP Erlestoke, in Wiltshire, have created their own artwork as part of the Prison Art Project scheme which is supported by homeless charity ALABARÉ. Participants are able to sell their work online with 50% of the proceeds going to the artist.

Many of the participants said creativity helped with their mental health and wellbeing while others said it felt "rewarding" to produce artwork.

Laura Joy, from the charity, said: "Artwork really gives people a chance to do meaningful activity towards rehabilitation and to support better choices."

Participants are provided with an art pack full of supplies like acrylics, pencils, watercolours and pastels with the condition that they create up to four pieces of artwork.

If their work is purchased, the artist receives half of the profits with the remainder used to fund the purchase of materials for others on the scheme.

The project has had more than 3,000 participants since it began in the 1960s.

There are currently 100 artists participating from 37 prisons and young offender institutions across England and Wales and more than 1,500 pieces of art were waiting to be uploaded and sold online.

Joy said the scheme was "a way of giving back" and a way to give the artists a "huge sense of pride".

She said: "We know how underfunded and overcrowded prisons are and there are not opportunities in some prisons for the people in prison to study art.

"I'm delighted that participants are having their artwork seen outside of their cells and internal art classes.

"Many of the pieces have some incredible personal stories behind them and capture a world view that is often hidden."

articles.title: 'It can be isolating' - how does hot weather impact anxiety?
articles.summary: Southampton woman Lauren has health anxiety that gets worse during the hot weather.
articles.body:
"When it's hot the air feels different in your lungs. Your brain just starts going, 'Something's different - and therefore bad' even though it's not."

The hot weather and high temperatures can trigger anxiety and other mental health problems, according to new research from Oxford University.

Lauren Murphy, from Southampton, has anxiety and agoraphobia, a disorder defined by an intense fear of feeling trapped.

The heat can trigger this feeling of panic, making her feel "really isolated" and like she cannot breathe.

"You end up overthinking every single sensation, even if it's a regular everyday occurrence," she says.

The 34-year-old has had anxiety for about a decade, but noticed it became worse after she became a parent and was diagnosed with ADHD.

"When you're an anxious person, especially with health anxiety, you're so much more in tune with your body," she says.

Then her anxiety also got worse as the heat got stronger, which she first noticed when she went on holiday abroad a few years ago, and the high temperatures made her feel like she could not breathe.

When similar conditions arrived in the UK, she says those fears returned.

"It really brought it all back. This year has probably been the worst." she said.

A fourth heatwave of the year is affecting parts of the UK , with a drought declared across large parts of England and the whole of Wales.

"Your heart might be beating faster, you're sweating more, and all of that feels so alarming when you're anxious," Lauren says.

She says those physical sensations - including a heavy feeling in her chest, a racing heart and difficulty concentrating - can reinforce the symptoms of anxiety, creating a cycle that is difficult to break.

"It's like anxiety's the main character and you're the ensemble."

Lauren is not alone - a 2022 study from the University of Bath estimated that about 4.6% of people , external in the UK had climate anxiety.

It is a form of mental distress recognised by professional bodies and the NHS, with young people and women among the groups most at risk, according to a 2025 study , external .

"Heat stress might feel like anxiety, they have the same physiological response," says Professor Ciara MaCabe, who works at the University of Reading and specialises in mental health.

"So the anxiety feelings are due to the heat, and then anxiety can kick in.

"The more heatwaves we have obviously more and more people are going to experience this."

Lauren says she has since found ways to calm herself when she starts to panic.

"Journaling helps - your mind can think so much faster than you can write. Writing slows everything down," she says.

She says tapping techniques help "ground" her as well as breathing exercises, yoga and being in nature.

Her advice to others experiencing anxiety is to ask for help.

"I always underestimate my ability to cope," she says.

"Being brave isn't the absence of fear. It's having that fear and doing it anyway."

articles.title: National Trust expands park by 32 hectares in Saltram
articles.summary: Former agricultural land is turned into a public park in Plymouth, the National Trust says.
articles.body:
Former agricultural land has been turned into additional public park space for people in Plymouth, the National Trust has said.

The 32 hectares (79 acres) of green space has "significantly" increased the size of the trust's land in Saltram and included a new 2.5km (1.5 mile) multi-use trail suitable for all users funded by Sport England through the National Lottery and the Trust, it said.

It added a series of rest stops had also been installed along the trail, offering "stunning views across Plymouth" and linking with Saltram's existing paths including The Dell.

National Trust Saltram general manager Jez McDermott said the opening was "a landmark moment" for Plymouth and Saltram.

He said: "This investment in access, wellbeing and nature means more people can enjoy everything Saltram has to offer.

"Whether you're walking, wheeling, cycling, spending time with family or simply taking a moment to enjoy the views, we hope Saltram East becomes a place that people return to for generations to come."

The trust said investments had been made to "boost the diversity" of nature and wildlife in the area and that it had planted new wildflower hay meadows across the site to create homes for wildlife.

It said it also planned to create a community forest by planting up to 12,000 trees in the coming winter.

The trust said the existing country park attracted about one million visits each year and it expected the additional land to provide "significant health and wellbeing benefits" for locals.

Lisa Dodd-Mayne, of Sport England, said access to nature "shouldn't be a luxury".

She said: "In a growing city like Plymouth, these new trails will make it easier for more people to build active travel into everyday life, get outdoors and enjoy the health and wellbeing benefits of green spaces close to home."

articles.title: Andrea Canning reports on the murder of Dee Warner in “The Day Dee Disappeared” | Dateline
articles.summary: Watch the Dateline episode “The Day Dee Disappeared” about the 2021 murder of Dee Warner in Lenawee County, Michigan.
articles.body: The life of a farmer is routine. Plant the seeds. Fertilize the soil. Harvest the crops. For 52-year-old Dee Warner, a sixth-generation farmer, that rhythm ran deep. Routine was a part of other aspects of her life too, including her standing Sunday morning breakfast date with her daughter Rikkell. But on April 25, 2021, when Rikkell arrived to meet her mother, Dee was nowhere to be found. Rikkell called her siblings to check if they had heard from her, but no one had. Then they called Dee’s husband, Dale. He said the last time he saw her was earlier that morning when she was asleep on the couch. Dee’s brother Gregg Hardy wasn’t worried, not at first. His sister often took a day or two away to think. But when his calls to Dee went straight to voicemail, he knew something wasn’t right. Dee always took Gregg’s calls or called right back. So Gregg and his wife, Shelley, volunteered to help search Dee’s property themselves. That’s when they grew even more concerned. Both of Dee’s cars were at the house. So where was Dee? It would take years to get an answer to that question. And the way that answer was discovered was just devastating. To find out what happened, watch the full episode of “The Day Dee Disappeared,” available now on Peacock. You can also watch on the NBC app or listen to the full episode on our podcast. Then watch loved ones remember Dee as a caring mother and supportive employer. Also, learn the history of one of the episode’s interview locations: Chaloner & Co., the oldest cigar store in Michigan. articles.title: Leo Wagner went missing in April 2021 in St. Mary, Montana | Dateline
articles.summary: Leo Wagner was last seen April 27, 2021, in St. Mary, Montana. Some of his clothing was later found near a cabin along Lower St. Mary Lake. The Blackfeet Law Enforcement Services are handling his case.
articles.body: “This case has torn my family apart,” Nicole Wagner told “Dateline.” “Our family will never be the same again, ever.” Her twin brother, Leo Wagner, has been missing for more than five years. The 26-year-old was last seen April 27, 2021, on the Blackfeet Indian Reservation in St. Mary, Montana. “What I hope for, in the future or in the present, is that my brother’s remains can be found, so we can lay him to rest the proper way,” Nicole said. Leo grew up in Browning, Montana, on the Blackfeet Indian Reservation. “He loved to play basketball. He loved to ride horses. He loved his family,” Nicole said. “He’s an outgoing person, happy and always smiling.” Nicole says that as an adult, her brother faced unbearable tragedy when one of his children died. “It was kind of tough for him,” she said. “Our family would check on him and stuff, just to keep an eye on him.” On April 14, 2021, Nicole visited Leo and noticed he didn’t seem like his normal self. “I could tell something was bothering him, and I kept asking him, but he wouldn’t tell me,” she said. Nicole remembers Leo asked her to stay longer, but she said she had to leave. “I’ll always regret that for the rest of my life.” Two weeks later, Leo disappeared. According to Nicole, on April 27, their father stopped by their mother’s house in Browning, where Leo was staying, to drop off some shirts for him. A group of people were at the house with Leo when their father arrived. Nicole told “Dateline” that Leo then put on a white tank top and one of the cowboy shirts their father had just brought. “Next thing you know, they leave, and that was the last time my dad seen Leo and my mom seen Leo,” she said. When Leo hadn’t returned home by the next day, the family called Blackfeet Law Enforcement Services (BLES) to report him missing. In the following days, the family was able to piece together some of what happened after Leo left the house after talking to members of the community. He apparently made a few stops at houses around town before driving to a gathering near Lower St. Mary Lake in St. Mary. The area is about 30 minutes from Browning. Nicole says she, her brother Billy and other family members searched that area in early May and discovered a cabin in disarray. “We see all the blood in the window. We see all the blood on the cabin, and then my dad and Billy find the sock and a shoe he was wearing,” she recalled. Nicole told “Dateline” she isn’t sure what happened in that cabin but believes Leo may have met with foul play. Shortly after that, Nicole went on Facebook to ask her community for help. “I called everybody out, and I lost my voice from yelling for Leo, and I couldn’t even talk,” she said. “And everybody was just coming out, flooding out there and everything, and I appreciated every single one of them.” The search widened from there. Nicole remembers private and volunteer dive teams going to St. Mary Lake to search for Leo. Nothing of note was found during those searches. On May 9, 2021, BLES told the public in a statement that it was scaling back search efforts for Leo the following day. “Blackfeet Fish & Wildlife will continue to search the area,” the statement read. NBC affiliate KULR of Billings reported on a news conference BLES held June 1, 2021. It said, “BLES said they searched approximately 70 square miles and multiple agencies assisted them.” BLES also laid out its timeline of Leo’s disappearance. “They said they responded to a call of someone under the influence walking the shore line of St. Mary’s Lake and when they got there, they couldn’t find the man or the caller,” KULR said. “An hour later, they were told the man was walking along West Shore Road with an injured arm.” West Shore Road is one of the main roads near the area Leo was last seen. During the same news conference, BLES officials revealed that on May 2, 2021, they responded to the cabin Nicole says her family found while searching for Leo. BLES said that the cabin looked burglarized, and as if someone had been injured there. KULR said BLES confirmed with family that clothing found at the scene belonged to Leo and then “a full scale search was issued.” Nothing further was found at that location. In June 2021, the Cascade County Sheriff’s Office was brought in to assist with the search for Leo at the lake using its brand-new side-scan sonar. The sheriff’s office posted on Facebook that “although side scan sonar is never a guarantee, it significantly increases the odds of locating drowning victims.” The search did not locate Leo. In early August 2021, NBC Montana reported that BLES announced that St. Mary Lake would be closed for nine days while it performed searches for Leo. Those searches also came up empty. Nicole says that in the years following Leo’s disappearance, communication with law enforcement has been challenging. She says the family has yet to receive an official update from BLES. “We never hear nothing back when we report something,” she said. “Like, they don’t call us, they don’t text us or nothing.” “Dateline” reached out to BLES to discuss the case and the family’s concerns but has not yet received a response. “Dateline” also has not heard back from the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Missing and Murdered Unit, which has the basic details of Leo’s case on its website. Last week, the Montana Justice Department issued a news release about a new statewide public service announcement to raise awareness about missing Indigenous people in the state. The PSA video features Leo, James Douglas Limberhand, Shacaiah Blue Harding and Ashley Loring Heavy Runner. “Behind every missing person is a family at home waiting for answers,” state Attorney General Austin Knudsen said in the release. “This tragedy has had a devastating impact on our tribal communities, and the Montana Department of Justice is committed to being part of the solution.” Related: “Dateline” learned about Leo’s case while working on the episode “Secrets in Big Sky Country” for Season 5 of the “Dateline: Missing in America” podcast series. Ashley Loring Heavy Runner disappeared from the Blackfeet Indian Reservation in Browning, Montana, in June 2017. Nicole says Leo’s face is still up on posters around Browning. “It’s sad that Leo’s kids look at those posters and, ‘Hi, Dad. I love you, Dad. Where you at, Dad?’” she said. So far, no one has that answer. But Nicole will not stop searching for the twin who she says will always be in her heart. “I love my brother a lot, and I do miss him.” Leo Wagner is 5-foot-7 with brown hair and eyes. At the time of his disappearance, he weighed 140 pounds. He was last seen wearing a blue-striped western shirt with a white tank top underneath, blue jeans and blue shoes. He has a tattoo of a “W” on his hand. He would be 31 years old today. If you have any information regarding the disappearance of Leo Wagner, please contact the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Missing and Murdered Unit at 1-833-560-2065.
